clinicalPearls: Fluid-filled, epithelial-lined cavities that are among the commonest causes of a discrete breast lump in perimenopausal women aged roughly 35 to 50.
Often present suddenly as a smooth, mobile, sometimes tender lump; multiple and bilateral cysts are frequent.
Regarded as an aberration of normal breast involution within the ANDI framework rather than a disease.
Ultrasound classification into simple, complicated and complex cysts guides management and determines the need for intervention.
A simple anechoic cyst with imperceptible walls and posterior enhancement is benign and needs no aspiration unless symptomatic.
Aspiration is indicated for painful or tense cysts; clear or green-brown fluid can be discarded without cytology.
Blood-stained aspirate, a residual mass after aspiration, or rapid refilling should prompt imaging and biopsy to exclude an intracystic carcinoma or papilloma.
Complex cysts with thick septa, mural nodules or solid components require image-guided core biopsy.
reference.pathophysiology: Breast cysts arise from the terminal duct lobular unit during the involutional phase of breast development, when lobular stroma regresses faster than its epithelium, leaving distended acini that coalesce into macroscopic fluid-filled spaces. The lining may be flattened atrophic epithelium or show apocrine metaplasia, the latter associated with cysts that secrete potassium-rich fluid and tend to recur. Hormonal fluctuation influences cyst formation, explaining their peak incidence in the perimenopausal years and regression after the menopause unless hormone replacement therapy is used.
additionalInvestigations: Mammography in the appropriate age group as part of triple assessment
Diagnostic or therapeutic needle aspiration of tense or symptomatic cysts
Cytology of aspirate only when blood-stained
Image-guided core biopsy of any solid or complex component
redFlags: Persistent palpable or sonographic mass after complete aspiration
Rapid symptomatic refilling of an aspirated cyst
Mural nodule or thick irregular septa on ultrasound
Associated skin tethering, nipple change or suspicious microcalcification
reference.prognosis: Simple cysts are benign with an excellent prognosis and only a marginal, if any, increase in future breast cancer risk. Recurrence after aspiration is common, but reassurance and symptom-directed management are usually sufficient.
pitfalls: Sending clear cyst fluid for cytology, which is low-yield and unnecessary
Failing to re-examine and image after aspiration to exclude a residual mass
Dismissing a complex cyst as simple and missing an intracystic carcinoma
Attributing a blood-stained aspirate to a traumatic tap and delaying biopsy
Overlooking that hormone replacement therapy can drive cyst formation after the menopause
references: Standard textbook of breast imaging and ultrasound classification
management: Reassure and observe simple anechoic cysts, which need no intervention unless symptomatic
Perform therapeutic needle aspiration for tense or painful cysts, discarding clear or green-brown fluid without cytology
Send aspirate for cytology only when blood-stained, and take an image-guided core biopsy of any solid or complex component
Confirm the diagnosis by triple assessment with ultrasound characterisation, adding mammography in the appropriate age group
Perform post-aspiration ultrasound to confirm resolution, with re-aspiration or biopsy for rapidly recurrent or residual masses
Refer complex cysts or intracystic solid lesions to a breast specialist to exclude malignancy
